FALSE. The claim that the Board cannot permit a later opening contradicts the express second branch of 6.04(7). The item does not prohibit the Board from requiring additional information.
FALSE. Board approval of the application is the specified trigger. Initial receipt of medication stock is not the trigger in this provision.

choice_reviews.finding: FALSE. 6.09(1)(a)2 gives the good-standing proof a three-month benchmark; paragraph3 gives the inspection a two-year benchmark. Applying the former to both documents is wrong.
FALSE. Two-month proof satisfies paragraph2, while a thirty-month inspection fails paragraph3. A home-state renewal cycle is not a substitute inspection freshness benchmark.
FALSE. Active home-state licensure and dated application documents are independent requirements. Current licensure does not make the thirty-month inspection current for this application.

TRUE. The two-month proof is within three months, and the inspection must have occurred within the preceding two years. The rationale retains the Board’s additional-inspection discretion under6.09(1)(b).

quality_axes.legal_correctness: The exact three-month proof and two-year inspection provisions were read. With other application components stipulated complete, one document meets the benchmark and the other does not; no assumption about equivalent home-state authorization changes that result.
quality_axes.scenario_realism: An application reviewer choosing which dated document to replace is a practical task. All alternatives assess the same two documents, avoiding unrelated licensing trivia.
quality_axes.decision_path_uniqueness: MA-REV-0022 asks whether separate Massachusetts nonresident authorization is needed before shipment. This case is already in the application process and separates two document ages. The replaced legacy representative had both documents outside their limits; the new condition changes which document needs replacement.

choice_reviews.finding: TRUE. 9.21(1) requires the secured prescription area, (2) adds appropriate CII storage, (6) assigns security/access responsibility to the MOR and pharmacist on duty, and (10) includes expired or return-pending stock. The answer restores both location and storage compliance.
FALSE. Removal from saleable stock does not remove security duties because9.21(10) expressly covers expired stock pending disposition.
FALSE. A locked front-store office remains outside the prescription area. Meeting one access-control feature cannot replace9.21(1)’s location requirement.
FALSE. The on-duty pharmacist has a current security responsibility under9.21(6). Logging a concern for the next MOR shift does not make the present storage compliant.

quality_axes.legal_correctness: The resident retail setting and absence of an already completed reverse-distribution transfer keep9.21 applicable. The on-duty pharmacist’s current responsibility is explicit; a routine day off does not require adjudicating the extended-absence MOR appointment rules.
quality_axes.scenario_realism: Return-pending stock stored by front-store staff is a credible workflow failure. The locked-office alternative is plausible but still misses the secured-prescription-area requirement.
quality_axes.decision_path_uniqueness: MA-REV-0080 requires retaining already secured expired stock in on-hand accounting; this case requires physical relocation and compliant storage now. MA-REV-0013 concerns simultaneous MOR appointments. CanonicalMA-Q-0102 shares security restoration but uses a broken cabinet and no-loss/reporting distinction; the present scope should be described as representative practice improvement, not a globally unprecedented security decision.

choice_reviews.finding: FALSE. The licensee or representative may sign the application, while6.10(2)(a)’s unavailable-MOR inventory-report substitute is an authorized staff pharmacist. A nonpharmacist owner’s application signature does not qualify as that report signature.

TRUE. The opening paragraph of6.10(2) calls for the licensee or duly authorized representative and the proposed new MOR to sign the application. The option chooses one of the stated licensee-side alternatives and does not require a separate representative if the licensee signs personally.

TRUE WITH STATED BOUNDARY. Serious illness is an expressly listed unavailability reason. The final stem says the authorized staff pharmacist actually participated in the inventory and the incoming MOR signed; the option uses the authorized staff report-signature route and Board notification at application submission. It does not claim that a staff signature alone replaces the application, the inventory attestation, or every required signature.

FALSE. An inventory report cannot replace the change application required by6.10(1)–(2). The other application components remain relevant; the option is not merely suggesting an additional inventory attachment.

TRUE. The attestation includes that the inventory report was filed with the pharmacy’s controlled-substance records. Submitting the application does not eliminate pharmacy custody of the actual report.

quality_axes.legal_correctness: All five choices were checked against the exact6.10(2) opening paragraph and6.10(2)(a). The final stem cures the previously raised missing-participation concern. The literal distinction between application, inventory report, and attestation remains visible; the selected answers are appropriate steps, not a declaration that these alone form a complete approved application.
quality_axes.scenario_realism: Serious illness preventing a departing manager’s handover signature is an expressly contemplated practice circumstance. The new-MOR and staff-pharmacist participation facts support a truthful handover record.
quality_axes.decision_path_uniqueness: MA-REV-0014 tests which schedules enter an ordinary handover inventory. This case stipulates the correct inventory scope and changes the departing MOR’s availability, permitting a staff-pharmacist report-signature route that is unavailable merely for convenience in canonicalMA-Q-0389.

choice_reviews.finding: FALSE. The name notice can be timely, but6.04(8) makes the pharmacy license nontransferable and6.11(2) separately requires the proposed new licensee’s application. An unchanged address does not transfer the seller’s permit.

FALSE. The name event occurred five days ago. Waiting until fourteen days before a sale six weeks away would miss6.12’s separate fourteen-day name-notice period. The future sale does not restart the earlier clock.

TRUE. 6.12 requires written name-change notice with authorizing documentation within fourteen days;6.11(1)–(2) imposes the seller notice and buyer application at least fourteen days before ownership transfer. The rationale preserves documentation and Board approval as separate from timely filing.
FALSE. The post-change fourteen-day name rule cannot be reused as the ownership filing rule. Both ownership duties are expressly at least fourteen days before transfer.

quality_axes.legal_correctness: The already-effective operating-name change and future transfer to a different legal entity trigger different directions of fourteen-day filing rules. The single correct sequence addresses both; it does not treat timely filing as approval or as fulfillment of stock-transfer requirements.
quality_axes.scenario_realism: Bundling administrative filings during a sale is plausible, and the proposed delay would concretely miss the earlier deadline. Alternatives have comparable two-step structures.
quality_axes.decision_path_uniqueness: MA-REV-0016 covers the sale obligations generally. CanonicalMA-Q-0390 covers rename-only notification andMA-Q-0362 covers the seller’s independent sale notice. This case combines a completed name change with a later sale so waiting for the later event would miss the earlier clock. The actual added event changes the required sequence; underlying rules are already represented elsewhere.
